worksheet.title: Meet the Blocks
worksheet.subtitle: A program is a stack of blocks
worksheet.learning_goal: I can find the GO block that starts a program.

parts.title: What is a program?
parts.text: A program is a stack of blocks that snap together. Bit runs the blocks from the TOP to the bottom, one at a time. The green ⚑ GO block always sits on top — it starts the program. The blue ➡ blocks tell Bit to move.

parts.title: Bit's program
parts.note: The green ⚑ block is on top, so it runs first and starts the program. Then Bit runs each blue ➡ block down the stack.

parts.title: Find the start
parts.prompt: Circle the block that STARTS Bit's program above. Hint: it is green and it sits on top.

parts.title: Which one is ready?
parts.prompt: A program is ready to run only if the green ⚑ GO block is on TOP. One stack is ready and one is not. Circle the stack that is ready — write A or B.

parts.title: You try
parts.prompt: The top block is empty. Draw a ⚑ in it and colour it green so Bit's program is ready to run.

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: Every program starts with the green ⚑ GO block on top. Then Bit runs each block down the stack, one at a time — that is how a computer follows a program.

teacher_guide.eyebrow: Teacher Guide · Kindergarten · Intro Block Coding
teacher_guide.title: Meet the Blocks
teacher_guide.subtitle: Quick facilitation notes & answer key

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Children learn that a program is a stack of blocks that snap together and run from the top down, and that the green GO block (the flag) always sits on top to start it. This is the first idea of block coding. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper, a pencil, and a crayon. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: paper blocks (a green flag block + arrow blocks) to stack by hand, or floor boxes the child can walk.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 15 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Point to a stack: "The blocks snap together and run from the top. The green flag GO block goes on top to start it."
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — circle the green GO block on top of Bit's program.
3. Let them try. Children pick the ready stack (Ex 2), then draw a green flag on top to make a stack ready (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — the start block is the green GO block (the flag) on top. Exercise 2 — Stack A is ready (the GO block is on top); Stack B is not (its top block is a move arrow).
Exercise 3 — draw a green flag in the top block; now the stack is ready to run.

parts.title: If children get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: picking any green block. The start block is the flag GO block, and it must be on TOP.
Make it easier: stack paper blocks by hand and put the flag on top.
Make it harder: ask what happens if the GO block is in the middle (the stack is not ready).
Make it active: have children be blocks and stack themselves with the GO child on top.

parts.title: Ontario Kindergarten link (official wording)
text: Problem Solving and Innovating — children recognize that coded instructions are assembled in order with a designated starting point.
In plain terms: a program is a stack of blocks that run from the top down; the green GO block starts it.
No reading is needed from the child — you read each prompt aloud; the child circles, numbers, or draws an arrow.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child finds the green GO block on top and makes a stack ready to run.
